A1.notes.Q3: Privacy is paramount, but some data *can* be helpful if it improves outcomes and doesn't disproportionately affect vulnerable groups.
A1.notes.Q4: Explainability is vital for trust and appropriate support. A black box model feels irresponsible, even if more accurate.
A1.notes.Q5: Fairness must be a key consideration; perpetuating inequalities isn't acceptable, even with slight gains in total help.
A1.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach and an open invitation are best – allowing students agency is key.
A1.notes.Q7: With a general email, erring on the side of more contacts is okay. But with personalized contact, be more selective – it's more intrusive.
A1.Q8.1: The model needs to consider students’ individual circumstances beyond academic performance—things like mental health or family commitments.

A2.notes.Q3: Privacy is paramount, especially with demographic data. Disability information warrants consideration for fairness but needs strong justification.
A2.notes.Q4: Explainability is vital for building trust with students. We need to understand *why* a student is flagged, especially when intervening directly.
A2.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial. A small decrease in overall identification to ensure equity across groups is acceptable; missing disadvantaged students exacerbates problems.
A2.notes.Q6: Personalized contact & advisor meetings are most effective. Too frequent outreach risks overwhelming students; twice a year feels manageable.
A2.notes.Q7: With generic emails, a broader net is okay. But personalized contact needs to be targeted – fewer students but more meaningful support.
A2.Q8.1: The survey focuses on data *used* by the model, but it's important to also consider how *we* interpret those results and avoid confirmation bias in our outreach.

A3.notes.Q3: Privacy is paramount, especially with demographic data. Only use if it significantly improves identification *and* addresses fairness concerns; even then proceed cautiously.
A3.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial for trust and appropriate intervention. A model I can’t explain feels like a black box - difficult to justify and hard to work with.
A3.notes.Q5: Fairness is vital. We can't exacerbate existing inequalities, even for overall gains in identification rates. Prioritizing recall makes sense - finding *all* struggling students is key.
A3.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach feels less intrusive and allows for targeted support. An invitation to meet offers the student agency.
A3.notes.Q7: Generic emails can be useful but risk being ignored; personalized contacts are more effective, even if fewer are made.
A3.Q8.1: It’s important to consider the resources needed for adequate follow-up. A highly accurate model is useless without staff time and support services.

S1.notes.Q3: I'm wary of data collection, especially after my dropout. Course performance is okay, but things like Absalon data feel too intrusive. Fairness needs to be considered for sensitive data.
S1.notes.Q4: Explainability is really important to me. I need to understand *why* a system thinks I'm struggling. A black box isn’t helpful, and makes me distrust the support offered.
S1.notes.Q5: Fairness is paramount, but a small loss in overall identification is acceptable if it means everyone gets equal attention. I don't want certain groups consistently overlooked.
S1.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach is better, but not too frequent! Twice a year seems reasonable – enough to be helpful without being overwhelming.
S1.notes.Q7: With generic emails, contacting more students isn’t as problematic. With personalized outreach the risk of unnecessary contact is higher, so a balance is needed.
S1.Q8.1: I'm concerned about creating self-fulfilling prophecies; being labeled 'at risk' might discourage someone. And there should be an easy opt-out mechanism.

S2.notes.Q3: Privacy is crucial, especially regarding sensitive data. Improvements must be substantial to justify including potentially invasive information. Nationality and financial aid might relate to support needs.
S2.notes.Q4: Explainability is key for trust and effective support, especially given I’m an international student navigating a new system. A large improvement needs to happen when stepping down in explainability.
S2.notes.Q5: Fairness is very important. Missing students who need help is worse than false positives, even if it requires a slight reduction in overall accuracy. Prioritize reaching those overlooked.
S2.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach is preferable, as generic messages can be easily ignored. A meeting offers a chance for real conversation, but twice per year strikes the right balance.
S2.notes.Q7: For general info, reaching more is okay; but with personalized help, quality matters more than quantity. We don't want to overwhelm advisors.
S2.Q8.1: It would be helpful to know how the model handles students like me – international students balancing studies and work. That context is important for effective support.

S3.notes.Q3: Privacy is crucial, but knowing students need help outweighs some risk for things like performance data. Disability info requires fairness gains.
S3.notes.Q4: Explainability is really important, especially for students with chronic conditions who might need to justify support requests. Accuracy tradeoffs are acceptable if trust suffers.
S3.notes.Q5: Fairness is paramount! Missing a student from any group because of the model is unacceptable. A small drop in overall accuracy is worth it for equitable support.
S3.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach shows care and avoids generic messaging. A meeting offers proper support discussion, but an email is a less intrusive first step. Twice yearly feels reasonable.
S3.notes.Q7: Personalized emails justify more selective outreach. Less intrusive, so can be slightly more selective than just blanket contact. General email should aim to reach almost all.
S3.Q8.1: The survey doesn't explicitly address the potential for false positives and their impact on student wellbeing - feeling 'flagged' could create anxiety.

S4.notes.Q3: Privacy is important, but acknowledging disability can help tailor support. It's frustrating seeing blanket 'never' options when data could be used responsibly.
S4.notes.Q4: Explainability is vital for trust, especially given my own experience navigating support systems. More opaque models feel controlling.
S4.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial; a model perpetuating inequality isn’t helpful. Some loss of overall accuracy is acceptable for equitable outcomes.
S4.notes.Q6: Personalized support matters. I’d want something tailored, not a generic message. Regular check-ins are good but not constant.
S4.notes.Q7: With emails, more reach is okay; with advisors' time, being selective is kinder to everyone. The personalised approach warrants a balanced response.
S4.Q8.1: The survey doesn’t address whether students will *know* they are being assessed by a model. Transparency about this process is critical for building trust.

S5.notes.Q3: I'm uneasy about sharing personal data, especially sensitive stuff like age or ethnicity. It needs a *very* good reason and the benefits need to clearly outweigh the risks, particularly given I’m an international student in a new system.
S5.notes.Q4: Explainability is important for trust and for being able to act on the information. If I don't understand *why* something is flagged, it’s hard to know what support I need or if it's even correct.
S5.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial. It's not okay for the system to be biased against certain groups, especially considering I’m an international student navigating a new academic culture. Missing some students is better than being unfair.
S5.notes.Q6: A generic email feels impersonal, and a meeting invitation is good but requires my time. Personalized emails seem like the best balance. Checking in twice a year feels appropriate, not too intrusive.
S5.notes.Q7: With generic email, reaching out to more is okay; with personalized contact, it's important to be mindful of people's time and avoid unnecessary intrusion.
S5.Q8.1: It feels like the focus has been on identifying struggles. What about proactively offering resources to *all* students – workshops on study skills, cultural adjustment, etc? – instead of just those flagged by a model?

S6.notes.Q3: Privacy is crucial, especially with sensitive data. Improvements must be significant to justify intrusions. Nationality & first-gen status seem less invasive than others.
S6.notes.Q4: Explainability is very important for trust and effective support. A high level of explainability is vital, even at a small cost in accuracy.
S6.notes.Q5: Fairness is non-negotiable. We must avoid exacerbating existing inequalities; even if it means less overall identification of struggling students.
S6.notes.Q6: Personalized contact is more valuable but must be carefully handled. Not too intrusive; twice a year seems reasonable and not overwhelming.
S6.notes.Q7: More targeted, personalised interventions justify being slightly less broad. Fewer false positives are important with such contact.
S6.Q8.1: The model needs to account for students who transfer *into* the university system, like myself. My previous dropout doesn't reflect my current potential. Context matters!

S7.notes.Q3: I'm wary of using too much personal data, but disability status feels relevant as long as it’s used to *help* fairness and not penalize students. Data from Absalon especially seems intrusive.
S7.notes.Q4: Explainability is important, especially given my learning difference. I'd want to know *why* I was flagged, not just *that* I was. A little less accuracy for more transparency seems worth it.
S7.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial. It's not okay if the model consistently misses students like me, or unfairly targets other groups. A small dip in overall accuracy is worth it to avoid bias.
S7.notes.Q6: Generic emails feel impersonal, and constant contact is overwhelming. A personalized email followed up by an optional meeting sounds like a good balance.
S7.notes.Q7: The more involved the intervention (personalized email/meeting), the more careful you need to be about false positives. I'd prefer fewer, better-targeted interventions.
S7.Q8.1: It would be good to understand how data is anonymized and secured, and if there's a way for students to opt out of the model entirely.

S8.notes.Q3: I'm cautious about data collection, but understand needing more info to help. Background is relevant for first-gen/financial aid.
S8.notes.Q4: Explainability is important for trust and effective support, but some loss of accuracy is acceptable if the explanations are useful.
S8.notes.Q5: Fairness is critical; a system that disadvantages already vulnerable groups isn't helpful. I’d rather reach fewer students equitably.
S8.notes.Q6: Personalized contact is best, and a meeting offers more support than just information. Twice a year feels like a good balance.
S8.notes.Q7: With generic emails, many false positives are okay. With personalized outreach from advisors, precision is more important.
S8.Q8.1: It would be good to know how the model will handle students who change programs or have complex situations - not a one-size-fits-all system.

S9.notes.Q3: Privacy is crucial, especially given my experience with managing a long-term condition. Data collection needs strong justification; a small benefit doesn't warrant intrusion.
S9.notes.Q4: Explainability builds trust, which is vital when dealing with potentially sensitive issues like academic struggles. I need to understand *why* a system thinks I'm at risk.
S9.notes.Q5: Fairness is paramount. Even if it means reaching fewer students overall, ensuring equitable support for all groups is essential – especially those already facing challenges.
S9.notes.Q6: A personalized approach is best, followed by a chance to talk things through. Constant outreach feels intrusive; twice a year seems reasonable.
S9.notes.Q7: I'd prefer fewer contacts if it means those are targeted and based on genuine need, especially with personalized support available. Less is more when it’s meaningful.
S9.Q8.1: The survey doesn't directly address the potential for stigma associated with being flagged by a predictive model. That worries me.
